lead: An NFA can have many runs on one input. The subset construction turns that choice into bookkeeping: after reading a string, the DFA remembers the set of all NFA states any run could be in. One deterministic state stands for a whole set. This removes nondeterminism without changing the accepted language. Compilers and text tools use it to turn pattern NFAs into fast DFA scanners. It also proves the central result that nondeterministic and deterministic finite automata accept exactly the same languages.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for NFA runs and 1.5 for ε-closures.

sections.h3: One DFA state holds a set

blocks.text: After reading a prefix, an NFA may sit in many states at once. The subset construction makes that whole set one DFA state. Two runs that end in the same set of NFA states have the same possible futures, so the set is enough memory. The DFA state space is Q_D = 2^{Q_N}, the set of all subsets of the NFA states.
δ_D(S, a) = ECLOSE( ∪_{p ∈ S} δ_N(p, a) )
blocks.where: S is a DFA state, a subset of Q_N; a is an input symbol; δ_N(p, a) is the set of NFA states p can enter on a; the union collects every state any run in S can reach; ECLOSE adds states reachable by ε-transitions; δ_D(S, a) is the next DFA state. ECLOSE(∅) = ∅.

blocks.text: The start state is q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}). The final states are F_D = { S ⊆ Q_N : S ∩ F_N ≠ ∅ }. A set is final when it contains at least one final NFA state, because the NFA accepts if some run accepts.

sections.h3: Build only what you can reach

blocks.text: Do not write all 2^n subsets. Start from q_D0 and follow transitions; only reachable subsets become states. This keeps the table small for real machines.

items: Find ECLOSE({p}) for every NFA state p, or compute ECLOSE on demand.
Set q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}) and mark it unprocessed.
Take an unprocessed subset S. For each symbol a in Σ, compute T = ECLOSE(∪_{p∈S} δ_N(p, a)).
Add the transition S --a--> T. If T is new, add it as a DFA state, including T = ∅ when it is reached.
Repeat until no unprocessed subset remains. Mark S final if S ∩ F_N ≠ ∅.

blocks.text: Claim: for every string w, δ̂_D(q_D0, w) = δ̂_N(q₀, w), where q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}) and δ̂_N(q₀, w) is the set of all NFA states reachable from q₀ by some run reading w. Base: w = ε. δ̂_D(q_D0, ε) = q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}) = δ̂_N(q₀, ε). Step: assume the claim for w. For symbol a, δ̂_D(q_D0, wa) = δ_D(δ̂_D(q_D0, w), a) = ECLOSE(∪_{p∈δ̂_N(q₀,w)} δ_N(p, a)) = δ̂_N(q₀, wa). The middle equality is the definition of δ_D; the last is one more NFA step followed by ε-closure.

So a string w is accepted by D exactly when δ̂_D(q_D0, w) meets F_N, which happens exactly when some NFA run on w ends in F_N. Hence L(D) = L(N). Equivalence means equal languages, not equal state counts.
Q_D has at most 2^n subsets, so D has at most 2^n states when N has n. This bound is achievable: some n-state NFAs need 2^n DFA states, so the blow-up is real, not loose counting.

Some syllabi first eliminate ε-transitions, then run subset construction on the ε-free NFA. The formula above folds ε-closure into each step, so it gives the same DFA. Reducing the result goes to 1.7.

spec.aria: A left-to-right flow from an NFA through epsilon-closures and reachable subsets to a DFA table and finally a minimal DFA.

examples.question: Convert the NFA N = ({q0,q1,q2}, {a,b}, δ, q0, {q2}) to a DFA using subset construction. The moves are: δ(q0,a)={q0,q1}, δ(q0,b)={q0}, δ(q1,a)=∅, δ(q1,b)={q2}, δ(q2,a)=δ(q2,b)=∅. Give the states, start state, final states and transition table.
steps: No state has ε-moves, so ECLOSE(S)=S for every subset S.
A on a: δ(q0,a)={q0,q1}, so B={q0,q1}. A on b: δ(q0,b)={q0}=A.
B on a: q0 gives {q0,q1}, q1 gives ∅, union {q0,q1}=B. B on b: q0 gives {q0}, q1 gives {q2}, union {q0,q2}=C.
C on a: q0 gives {q0,q1}, q2 gives ∅, union B. C on b: q0 gives {q0}, q2 gives ∅, union A.
No new subsets. Q_D={A,B,C}. Final states: only C contains q2, so F_D={C}.
Transition table: A-a B, A-b A, B-a B, B-b C, C-a B, C-b A.
examples.answer: The DFA has 3 states A, B, C, start A, final C, and 6 transitions; it accepts exactly the strings over {a,b} that end in ab.
examples.check:
from collections import deque

delta = {('q0','a'): {'q0','q1'}, ('q0','b'): {'q0'},
         ('q1','a'): set(), ('q1','b'): {'q2'},
         ('q2','a'): set(), ('q2','b'): set()}

start = frozenset({'q0'})
seen = {start}
q = deque([start])
trans = 0
while q:
    S = q.popleft()
    for c in 'ab':
        T = frozenset().union(*[delta.get((p, c), set()) for p in S])
        trans += 1
        if T not in seen:
            seen.add(T)
            q.append(T)
print(len(seen))
print(trans)

traps: A subset is final if it contains at least one final state. It need not consist only of final states.
Apply ECLOSE after every move, not just at the start. The formula closes the union of moves.
Include the empty subset ∅ as a dead state if a transition reaches it; do not drop the transition.
Do not list subsets that cannot be reached from the start. The DFA states are reachable subsets only.
Equivalence means L(D)=L(N). The DFA can have more states; do not mark an answer wrong for a larger but correct DFA.

quiz.q: Define the start state of the subset-construction DFA for NFA N with start q₀.
quiz.a: q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}), the ε-closure of the set containing only q₀.

quiz.q: Why is a subset final when it intersects F_N?
quiz.a: The NFA accepts if at least one run reaches a final state. The subset lists all possible runs, so an intersection means some run is final.

quiz.q: Using the worked example, compute δ_D(B,b).
quiz.a: B={q0,q1}. q0 on b gives {q0}; q1 on b gives {q2}; union {q0,q2}=C. No ε-moves, so δ_D(B,b)=C.

quiz.q: Why can subset construction need exponentially many states?
quiz.a: Each DFA state is a subset of n NFA states, and all 2^n subsets can be reachable in worst-case NFAs; each subset may need distinct future behaviour.

quiz.q: NFA states q0,q1,q2 have ε-moves q0→q1 and q1→q2. Find ECLOSE({q0}).
Does L(D)=L(N) require D and N to have the same number of states?
quiz.a: No. It requires the same accepted language; state counts may differ.

quiz.q: Why build only reachable subsets instead of all 2^n?
quiz.a: Unreachable subsets can never be entered from the start, so they cannot affect acceptance; omitting them gives the same language with far fewer states.

beyond: Not for the exam. Subset construction is the bridge from regular expressions to scanners in compilers: a pattern becomes an NFA, then a DFA table drives the lexer. Hardware and network intrusion detection sometimes compile patterns to DFAs for one-pass matching. Model checkers use the same subset idea to determinise automata over infinite traces. Search for 'powerset construction', 'NFA to DFA lexer', and 'DFA state blow-up'.
